mainTopic: When rumors force a divorce, remarrying a wife divorced for a bad name, and why an agent or a death witness may not marry the woman he freed
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא about suspicious signs in the home. רבי says that if reversed shoe prints are found under the bed, the wife must be divorced because the matter is ugly. The גמרא rules like both רב, who requires witnesses, and רבי. It settles the clash this way: a rumor (קלא) that keeps going is enough on its own, but a rumor that stops needs עדים. אביי says a persistent rumor lasts a day and a half. The גמרא then adds limits about a pause in the talk, a pause caused by fear, and enemies who may have started the rumor. Next, רבה בר הונא asks whether a man who divorced his wife for a bad name and then remarried her must divorce her again. A proof from the suspected-adulterer משנה is rejected, because his marrying her strengthens the rumor while the husband's taking her back weakens it. A new משנה then says that an agent who brings a גט from overseas, or a witness to the husband's death, may not marry the woman. The גמרא explains that a גט is a written document that proves itself, unlike a death report. Finally, the גמרא questions how anyone may rely on a witness who says 'I killed him,' since he has called himself a רשע. Its rejection of the idea that עדות אשה is more lenient continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Reversed shoes under the bed
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if the husband finds shoes turned around under the bed, רבי says she must leave because the matter is ugly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If shoes were found turned around under the bed, רבי said: since this is an ugly matter, she must be divorced.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא that lists suspicious signs in the house. Here רבי says that reversed shoes under the bed are enough to force a divorce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shoes facing the bed suggest a stranger came in and took them off there. רבי does not demand witnesses to an actual sin. For him, a disgraceful situation like this is enough to end the marriage.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter is ugly or disgraceful
She must leave, meaning she must be divorced

phrases.english: Shoes turned around under the bed,
phrases.notes: Turned around means the toes face the bed, as if someone climbed in and left them there.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי: הוֹאִיל וּמְכוֹעָר הַדָּבָר — תֵּצֵא.
phrases.english: Rabbi said: Since the matter is ugly, she must leave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from before this section, listing signs of possible adultery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי, a disgraceful sign like reversed shoes under the bed requires the wife to be divorced.

steps.title: Why not just check whose shoes they are?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the case: if there are real shoes, the husband can simply find out who owns them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reversed shoes? Let him look and see whose they are!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is questioning how the case in the ברייתא works. If actual shoes are lying there, the husband can identify the owner and clear up what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling 'since the matter is ugly' only makes sense if the situation stays unclear. Real shoes could be traced to their owner, so the uncertainty would go away. That makes the case as written seem odd.

phrases.english: Reversed shoes?
Let him see whose they are!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the facts of the case in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of reversed shoes in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Actual shoes can be identified, so the situation is not truly unclear and should be checked rather than ruled on as suspicious.

steps.title: It means shoe prints, not shoes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is about the marks or prints of reversed shoes, which cannot be traced to anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is the place of reversed shoes (under the bed; רבי said: since this is an ugly matter, she must leave).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא re-reads the ברייתא: it was only the prints of the shoes that were found, not the shoes themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Footprints cannot be matched to a specific person, so the husband has no way to check. The suspicion stays, and so רבי's ruling makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: The place of the shoes, meaning shoe prints

phrases.english: Rather: the place of reversed shoes
phrases.notes: He means the marks the shoes left, which can't be traced to anyone.

phrases.english: (under the bed, Rabbi said:
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets, since they just repeat the end of the case from above.

phrases.english: since the matter is ugly, she must leave).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2 by redefining the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא spoke about real shoes, which could be identified.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא speaks about shoe prints, which cannot be identified, so the suspicion remains.

steps.title: The ruling follows both רב and רבי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the הלכה follows רב and also follows רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is like רב, and the הלכה is like רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a final ruling that seems to agree with two different views at once. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב, mentioned earlier, requires witnesses before the wife must be divorced. רבי says a disgraceful situation is enough even without witnesses. Ruling like both sounds contradictory, and the גמרא is about to point that out.

phrases.english: And the halakha is like Rav,
phrases.notes: רב's view from earlier: she must be divorced only if there are witnesses.

phrases.english: and the halakha is like Rabbi.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַב, וְהִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After clarifying רבי's case, the גמרא gives the practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows both רב (witnesses) and רבי (an ugly matter).

steps.title: The two rulings contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that one ruling clashes with the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: One הלכה contradicts the other הלכה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that ruling like רב and like רבי seems impossible, because they disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב needs witnesses, while רבי does not. You cannot normally follow both views in the same case.

phrases.english: One halakha is difficult against the other halakha:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the double ruling of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the הלכה follows both רב and רבי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב requires witnesses and רבי does not, so the two rulings cannot both hold.

steps.title: A rumor that stops versus a rumor that keeps going
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction: רבי's rule applies when the rumor does not stop, and רב's rule applies when the rumor stops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about a rumor that stops, and that one is about a rumor that does not stop. With a rumor that does not stop and no witnesses, follow רבי. With a rumor that stops and there are witnesses, follow רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that each ruling is for a different situation, depending on whether the rumor (קלא) dies down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If talk about the woman keeps going, the divorce is required even without עדים, like רבי. If the talk dies down, the divorce is required only when there are עדים, like רב. So the two rulings fit together.
steps.whatToRemember: A rumor that keeps going is enough on its own, like רבי. A rumor that stops needs עדים, like רב.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is with a rumor that stops,
that one is with a rumor that does not stop.

phrases.aramaic: קָלָא דְלָא פָּסֵיק וְלֵיכָּא עֵדִים — כְּרַבִּי.
phrases.english: A rumor that does not stop and there are no witnesses: like Rabbi.
A rumor that stops and there are witnesses: like Rav.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא בְּקָלָא דְּפָסֵיק, הָא בְּקָלָא דְלָא פָּסֵיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rulings apply to the same situation and clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי's ruling covers a persistent rumor; רב's ruling covers a rumor that stopped, where witnesses are needed.

steps.title: How long must a rumor last?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long a rumor must continue to count as one that 'does not stop.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And a rumor that does not stop: for how long?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a measure of time, so we can know which rumors count as persistent. This sets up אביי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 6 depends on telling a stopping rumor from a persistent one. Without a time measure, that rule cannot be applied.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to how much? For how long?

phrases.english: And a rumor that does not stop, for how long?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the term used in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The length of time a rumor must last to count as persistent.

steps.title: A day and a half
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports in the name of his mother that town talk counts as persistent if it lasts a day and a half.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: My mother told me: talk in a town lasts a day and a half.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question: a rumor that lasts a day and a half counts as one that does not stop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary gossip in a town fades quickly. If it is still going after a day and a half, it is treated as a real, persistent rumor.

phrases.english: Abaye said: My mother told me:
phrases.notes: אביי often quotes 'mother' this way; it refers to the woman who raised him.

phrases.english: The talk of the town lasts a day and a half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A rumor that lasts a day and a half counts as persistent.

steps.title: First limit: the rumor must not pause
steps.stepSummary: The day and a half counts only if the rumor did not stop in the middle; if it paused, it counts as a rumor that stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when it did not stop in between. But if it stopped in between, it has stopped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a first limit to אביי's rule: the day and a half must be continuous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the talk died down and then started again, it is not one steady rumor. It is treated as a rumor that stopped, so רב's rule applies and witnesses are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, introducing a limit

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן, אֶלָּא דְּלָא פְּסַק בֵּינֵי וּבֵינֵי,
phrases.english: And we only said this when it did not stop in the meantime,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל פְּסַק בֵּינֵי וּבֵינֵי — הָא פְּסַק.
phrases.english: but if it stopped in the meantime, then it has stopped.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן, אֶלָּא דְּלָא פְּסַק בֵּינֵי וּבֵינֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits אביי's day-and-a-half rule from step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rumor that paused during the day and a half counts as a rumor that stopped.

steps.title: Second limit: a pause out of fear doesn't count
steps.stepSummary: A pause counts only if it was not caused by fear; if people stopped talking out of fear, the rumor is still persistent.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when it did not stop because of fear. But if it stopped because of fear, it is just because of fear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to the limit: a pause caused by fear does not break the rumor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If people went quiet because they were afraid of the person involved, the rumor did not really die. It still counts as a rumor that does not stop.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא פְּסַק מֵחֲמַת יִרְאָה,
phrases.english: And we only said this when it did not stop because of fear,
but if it stopped because of fear,
it is only because of fear.
phrases.notes: In other words, the silence is just fear, so the rumor still counts as going on.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא פְּסַק מֵחֲמַת יִרְאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the limit of step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pause caused by fear does not stop the rumor.

steps.title: Third limit: no weight if there are enemies
steps.stepSummary: A persistent rumor counts only if the person has no enemies; if he does, we assume the enemies spread it.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when there are no enemies. But if there are enemies, it is the enemies who put out the rumor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a final limit: a rumor carries no weight if the person has enemies who could have started it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a long-running rumor may be a lie spread by people who hate him. When there are known enemies, we blame the rumor on them and ignore it.
steps.whatToRemember: A persistent rumor (a day and a half, with no real pause) forces a divorce, but a pause out of fear doesn't break it, and a rumor that enemies could have started is ignored.

phrases.english: And we only said this when there are no enemies,
but if there are enemies,
it is the enemies who put out the rumor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third limit on when a persistent rumor counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rumor about someone with enemies is assumed to come from them and carries no weight.

steps.title: New topic: no taking back a wife divorced for a bad name or a vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: a man who divorces his wife because of a bad reputation or because of a vow may not take her back.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned there: One who divorces his wife because of a bad name may not take her back. Because of a vow, he may not take her back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a משנה from elsewhere. This sets up the question that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a man divorced his wife because of a שם רע or a נדר of hers, he is not allowed to remarry her later. This is the base rule for the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: He may not take her back

phrases.english: We learned there: One who divorces his wife
phrases.notes: The משנה is in גיטין 45b.

phrases.english: because of a bad name may not take her back.
Because of a vow, he may not take her back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic, related to the earlier theme of divorce over suspicion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who divorced his wife for a bad name or a vow may not remarry her.

steps.title: If he remarried her anyway, must he divorce her?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר הונא asks רבה בר רב נחמן: if the man went ahead and remarried her, must he divorce her again?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר הונא sent to רבה בר רב נחמן: Let our teacher teach us: if he married her, must he divorce her?
steps.whatsHappening: A question is sent about the משנה just quoted: what happens after the fact if the man broke the rule and remarried her. The answer comes later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says he may not take her back, but it doesn't say what to do if he already did. The question is whether the marriage must be broken up or may stay as it is.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Huna sent to him,
to Rabba bar Rav Naḥman:
Let our teacher teach us:
If he married her, must he divorce her?
phrases.notes: He means he remarried the wife he wasn't allowed to take back.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר הוּנָא לְרַבָּה בַּר רַב נַחְמָן, יְלַמְּדֵנוּ רַבֵּינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks a follow-up question on the משנה quoted in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a man who remarried a wife he was not allowed to take back must divorce her.

steps.title: Answer from the משנה about the suspected adulterer
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב נחמן answers that we already learned this: in the case of one suspected with a married woman, even if he married her he must divorce her.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We already learned this. If a man is suspected of being with a married woman, and she was sent out from her husband, then even if the suspected man married her, he must divorce her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב נחמן answers the question from step 13 by pointing to an earlier משנה. That משנה says that even after the marriage has happened, it must be broken up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was: if a man remarried a wife he divorced because of a bad name, must he divorce her again? רבה בר רב נחמן points out that the משנה already says 'even if he married her, he must divorce her' in the case of the suspected adulterer. He assumes the same applies here.

keyTerms.meaning: He must divorce her (literally, send her out)

phrases.english: He said to him: We already learned it:
phrases.notes: This is רבה בר רב נחמן answering רבה בר הונא's question from the last step.

phrases.english: One who is suspected regarding a married woman
and he sent her out from under his hand,
phrases.notes: Here 'his hand' is the husband's, meaning she was divorced from her husband.

phrases.english: even if he married her, he must divorce her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, he must divorce her again, just as the משנה rules for the suspected adulterer: 'even if he married her, he must divorce her.'

steps.title: The two cases use different wording
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר הונא rejects the proof: that משנה says 'they sent her out' (the court), but ours says 'he sent her out' (on his own).
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Are the cases really alike? There it says 'they sent her out,' and here it says 'he sent her out.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר הונא says the proof does not fit, because the two משניות use different wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the suspected-adulterer case the משנה says 'they' (the court) forced her out, so the case is stricter. In our case the husband divorced her on his own. Maybe a strict rule for a court-forced divorce does not carry over to a divorce the husband chose himself.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent her out (on his own)

phrases.english: He said to him: Is it comparable?
There, it says 'they sent her out,'
phrases.notes: 'There' is the משנה about the suspected adulterer, where the court makes them separate.

phrases.english: and here, it says 'he sent her out.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the two משניות
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: One case is a divorce forced by the court and the other is the husband's own choice, so they may not follow the same rule.

steps.title: רבה בר רב נחמן's version also reads 'he sent her out'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבה בר רב נחמן's text of the משנה also read 'he sent her out,' so in his view the two cases match.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה בר רב נחמן? In the משנה we also learned 'he sent her out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבה בר רב נחמן saw no difference: his copy of the משנה had the same wording as ours.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection in step 15 depended on the wording 'they sent her out.' If the משנה actually reads 'he sent her out,' then both cases are a husband divorcing on his own, and that objection falls away.

phrases.english: And רבה בר רב נחמן, how does he see it?
In the משנה too, we learned 'he sent her out.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּה בַּר רַב נַחְמָן, מַתְנִיתִין נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording objection of step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה says 'they sent her out,' a divorce forced by the court.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבה בר רב נחמן's version says 'he sent her out,' so both cases are the same kind of divorce.

steps.title: Husband versus the adulterer
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר הונא asks again: our case is the husband taking her back, but the משנה is about the man suspected of adultery marrying her.
steps.simpleTranslation: But still, are they alike? Here it is the husband, and there it is the man suspected of being with her!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר הונא raises a second difference between the cases: who is marrying her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our question the original husband remarries her. In the משנה the suspected adulterer marries her. These are very different people, so the rule for one may not apply to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: The man who (supposedly) was with her

phrases.english: But still, is it comparable?
Here it is the husband, and there it is the man who was with her!
phrases.notes: 'Here' is our question about the husband; 'there' is the משנה about the suspected adulterer.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַכַּתִּי מִי דָּמֵי? הָכָא בַּעַל, וְהָתָם בּוֹעֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the wording problem is solved, a new difference between the cases is raised.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule against the adulterer marrying her may not apply to the original husband taking her back.

steps.title: Both cases share the same pattern
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב נחמן answers that the two cases are alike: in both, the חכמים said 'he may not marry her, and if he did, he must divorce her.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: They are very much alike. Here the חכמים said: he may not marry her, and if he married her he must divorce her. So too the חכמים said: he may not take her back, and if he married her he must divorce her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב נחמן defends his comparison by showing that both rules have the same structure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both rules are rabbinic bans on marrying this woman. Since the חכמים forced a divorce in the adulterer case, he argues they meant the same in the husband case.

keyTerms.meaning: He may not take her back

steps.confusionAlert: Careful: in this step 'here' (הָכָא) means the suspected-adulterer משנה, not the husband's case as in step 17.

phrases.english: He said to him: They are very much alike.
Here the חכמים said:
phrases.notes: 'Here' now points to the suspected-adulterer משנה.

phrases.english: he may not marry her, and if he married her, he must divorce her.
So too the חכמים said,
he may not take her back, and if he married her, he must divorce her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the husband-versus-adulterer challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the two rules have the same structure
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The husband and the adulterer are different, so the rules may differ.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are bans by the חכמים, and the 'if he married, he must divorce' part carries over.

steps.title: The comparison fails: one strengthens the rumor, the other shows it was false
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison: the adulterer marrying her makes the rumor stronger, but a husband taking her back shows he checked the rumor and found it false.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not so. There, he makes the rumor stronger. Here, we say he looked into the rumor and found it was not true.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא itself rejects רבה בר רב נחמן's comparison, so the question from step 13 is left without a proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the suspected man marries her, people see it as proof of the rumor, so he must divorce her. When the husband takes her back, it suggests he checked and found the rumor baseless. So there is no reason to force a second divorce from this source.
steps.whatToRemember: The adulterer marrying her strengthens the rumor, so he must divorce her. The husband taking her back weakens it, so the משנה about the adulterer is no proof for the husband, and the question stays open.

phrases.english: But that is not so.
There, he made the rumor stronger,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the suspected man marrying her. People will say, 'See, the rumor was true.'

phrases.english: here, we say
he looked into the rumor and it was not true.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא הִיא. הָתָם: אַלּוֹמֵי אַלְּמֵיהּ לְקָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 18 and ends the discussion.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the suspected-adulterer משנה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In one case the marriage strengthens the rumor, and in the other it shows the rumor was false.

steps.title: The agent who brings a גט from overseas may not marry the woman
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: an agent who brings a גט from overseas and says 'it was written and signed in my presence' may not marry the divorced woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who brings a גט from overseas and says, 'It was written in front of me and signed in front of me,' may not marry that man's wife.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a new rule: someone whose own statement makes the divorce valid may not then marry the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גט from overseas is accepted because of the agent's statement. If he married her, it would look like he said it for his own benefit, so he is not allowed to marry her.

keyTerms.meaning: It was written in front of me and signed in front of me

phrases.english: משנה: One who brings a גט from overseas,
and said: 'It was written in front of me and signed in front of me,'
may not marry his wife.
phrases.notes: 'His wife' means the wife of the man who sent the גט, the woman now divorced.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An agent whose statement makes a גט from overseas valid may not marry the divorced woman.

steps.title: A witness to the husband's death may not marry the widow
steps.stepSummary: The same applies to one who testifies 'he died,' 'I killed him,' or 'we killed him': he may not marry the man's wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'He died,' 'I killed him,' or 'We killed him,' he may not marry the man's wife.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the same rule to a witness whose testimony about the husband's death lets the woman remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are three kinds of testimony that the husband is dead. In all of them, the man who testified is the one freeing her, so he may not benefit by marrying her.

phrases.english: If he said: 'He died,' 'I killed him,' or 'We killed him,'
he may not marry his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the rule of step 20 from a גט to testimony about death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A witness who testifies that the husband died, or that he or they killed him, may not marry the widow.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: 'I killed him' does not free her, 'We killed him' does
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that if he testified 'I killed him,' the wife may not remarry at all, but if he said 'we killed him,' she may remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If he said 'I killed him,' his wife may not remarry. If he said 'We killed him,' his wife may remarry.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion in the משנה about the testimony 'I killed him.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, 'I killed him' is not accepted as testimony at all, so the woman cannot remarry anyone. 'We killed him' is accepted, so she may remarry, though still not to these witnesses.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה's 'his wife may not be married' is not just about this witness. It means she may not marry anyone based on this testimony.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says:
'I killed him': his wife may not be married,
'We killed him': his wife may be married.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion of step 21 about 'I killed him.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, 'I killed him' does not free the wife at all, while 'we killed him' does free her to remarry.

steps.title: The ban applies only when the court relies on the agent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that the agent is barred only when the גט comes from overseas, where the court relies on his statement. An agent bringing a גט from ארץ ישראל may marry her.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that the גט came from overseas, where we rely on him. But if it came from ארץ ישראל, where we do not rely on him, he may marry the woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה's ban exists by pointing to the case it describes: a גט brought from overseas. From that, it concludes that an agent bringing a גט from ארץ ישראל may marry her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From overseas, the agent must say 'it was written and signed in my presence,' and the court relies on those words. If he then marries her, people could suspect he lied so he could have her. From ארץ ישראל no such statement is needed, so the גט stands on its own and nobody would suspect him.

keyTerms.meaning: A country overseas, outside ארץ ישראל
He may marry the man's wife (here, the divorced woman)

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The reason is that it is from overseas,
since we rely on him.
But from ארץ ישראל,
where we do not rely on him,
phrases.notes: Inside ארץ ישראל the agent does not have to make any statement, so the court is going only by the written גט.

phrases.english: he may marry his wife.
phrases.notes: 'His wife' means the divorcing husband's wife, the woman who just got the גט.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה from step 20 by explaining the reason for its ban.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The agent is barred from marrying the woman only when the court relies on his statement (a גט from overseas). From ארץ ישראל he may marry her.

steps.title: But the death witness is barred even though we don't rely only on him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges step 23 from the case of 'he died.' A woman checks carefully before remarrying, so the court does not rely only on the witness, yet the משנה still bars him from marrying her.
steps.simpleTranslation: But in the case of 'he died,' we do not rely only on him, as the Master said that a woman checks carefully and then marries. Yet the משנה teaches that he may not marry the man's wife!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason given in step 23. It points to a case in the same משנה that seems to break that rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 said the ban applies only when the court relies on the person's statement. When a witness says the husband died, the woman herself checks carefully before remarrying, so the court is not relying on him alone. Yet the משנה still bars him, which suggests that the reason in step 23 is not the real reason.

keyTerms.meaning: But look, this case (opens a challenge)
A woman checks carefully and only then remarries
And yet it teaches (in the משנה)

phrases.english: But in the case of 'he died,'
where we do not rely on him,
as the Master said:
A woman checks carefully and then marries,
and yet it teaches: He may not marry his wife!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 23 by using the death case from step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ban applies only when the court relies on the person's statement.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In a death report the court does not rely on the witness alone, because the woman checks for herself, yet the משנה still bars him. So reliance cannot be the deciding factor.

steps.title: A death report has no document, but a גט does
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the cases are different. In a death report there is no written document, while a גט is a written document that proves itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, there is no writing. Here, there is writing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends step 23 by showing a real difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the woman checks for herself, the death report still rests on a spoken statement with nothing written to back it up, so the witness stays under suspicion. A גט from ארץ ישראל is a document that stands on its own, so the agent who brings it is not suspected at all.

phrases.english: There, there is no writing,
here, there is writing.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם לֵיכָּא כְּתָבָא, הָכָא אִיכָּא כְּתָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (a written document versus spoken testimony)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the court does not rely on the person alone in either case, the death witness and the agent from ארץ ישראל should be treated the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: A גט is a written document that proves itself, so the agent who brings it from ארץ ישראל is not suspected. A death report has no document, so the witness may not marry her.

steps.title: A משנה proves that the writing makes the difference
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up its answer with a משנה that says the difference between a גט and a death report is that the writing proves the matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: What is the difference between a גט and death? The writing proves it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to show that its answer in step 25 is not just a guess.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That משנה already treats a גט and a death report differently, and the reason it gives is that the writing proves the matter. This is exactly the distinction step 25 used. So the idea that a document removes suspicion comes from an earlier source.

phrases.english: As we learned:
What is the difference between a גט and death?
phrases.notes: This משנה is about people who are believed when they bring a גט but not when they report a death.

phrases.english: That the writing proves it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 25 with an earlier source.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a גט is treated more leniently than a death report because it is written.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה 'מה בין גט למיתה, שהכתב מוכיח.'
steps.whatToRemember: A גט is a document that speaks for itself, and a death report is only spoken words. This is why the agent who brings a גט from ארץ ישראל may marry the woman, but the death witness may never marry her.

steps.title: Only the witness himself may not marry her, so others may
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the death cases from the משנה again and infers that only the witness himself may not marry the widow. Anyone else may marry her based on his testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He died,' 'I killed him,' 'we killed him': he may not marry the man's wife. He is the one who may not marry her, which implies that she may marry someone else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the death cases in the משנה and draws a careful inference from the wording. This prepares the next step, where the גמרא will examine whether that inference fits every case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only says that he, the witness, may not marry her. This implies that his testimony is accepted and she may marry another man. That is surprising for 'I killed him,' since a man who says he committed murder is calling himself wicked, and step 22 had רבי יהודה say she may not remarry at all in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: This implies she may marry someone else

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this line as the משנה being taught all over again. The גמרא is quoting it to make an inference: only the witness is barred, so other men may marry her.

phrases.english: 'He died,' 'I killed him,' 'we killed him':
he may not marry his wife.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא נִיהוּ דְּלֹא יִשָּׂא אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ,
phrases.english: It is he who may not marry his wife,
which implies that she may marry someone else.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא נִיהוּ דְּלֹא יִשָּׂא אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ, הָא לְאַחֵר תִּנָּשֵׂא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the גט discussion and returns to the death cases from step 21 to draw a new inference.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the witness himself is barred from marrying the widow. His testimony is accepted, so she may marry another man.
steps.whyThisMatters: This inference treats even 'I killed him' as testimony that lets her remarry. That clashes with רבי יהודה's view in step 22 and sets up the coming discussion.

steps.title: A witness who admits sinning should be disqualified
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges step 27 using רב יוסף's rule. A person who testifies that he willingly sinned is a רשע, and the תורה disqualifies a רשע as a witness. A man who says 'I killed him' should be disqualified the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב יוסף say: if a man testifies, 'So-and-so sodomized me against my will,' he and another witness join together to put the sinner to death. But if he says 'willingly,' he is a רשע, and the תורה said: 'Do not put your hand with the wicked to be a corrupt witness'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea from step 27 that people may rely on a witness who says 'I killed him.' It brings רב יוסף's rule that a person who admits his own sin cannot be a witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב יוסף's case, if the man was forced, he did nothing wrong, so he counts as a valid witness. If he went along willingly, his own words make him a רשע, and the פסוק disqualifies a רשע from testifying. A man who says 'I killed him' is also admitting a terrible sin, so his testimony should be thrown out, and the widow should not be allowed to remarry on his word.

keyTerms.meaning: Against my will, by force. He was a victim, so he did no sin.
Willingly. He took part in the sin himself.
They join together, meaning two witnesses combine to make a full pair of עדים.
A wicked person, someone who sinned on purpose. He is not allowed to be a witness.
A corrupt witness. The פסוק uses this phrase to disqualify a רשע from testifying.

steps.confusionAlert: The case of רביעה here is only an example. The real point is the general rule that a man who admits he sinned becomes a רשע and loses his right to testify. That rule is what the גמרא applies to 'I killed him.'

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yosef say:
"So-and-so sodomized me against my will" —
he and another combine to put him to death.
phrases.notes: "Another" means a second witness who saw it. Together they make the two witnesses needed for a death penalty.

phrases.english: "Willingly" — he is wicked,
and the Torah said:
"Put not your hand with the wicked
phrases.notes: שמות 23:1

phrases.english: to be a corrupt witness"?
phrases.notes: The unspoken point: a man who says "I killed him" also makes himself a רשע, so he should not be trusted either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference of step 27 that others may marry the widow based on the testimony 'I killed him.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that a witness who says 'I killed him' is believed, so the widow may marry someone else.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By רב יוסף's rule, admitting a sin makes a person a רשע, and a רשע is disqualified as a witness. Saying 'I killed him' admits to murder, so the testimony should not count at all.

steps.title: Blocking the idea that the רבנן were lenient for a woman's testimony
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a possible answer: testimony that frees a woman to remarry is different, because the רבנן were lenient with it. It immediately starts to reject that answer by bringing רב מנשה, whose statement comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that testimony for a woman is different, since the רבנן were lenient with it, didn't רב מנשה say:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible way out of the challenge: in עדות אשה the רבנן relaxed the usual rules for witnesses. It then sets up its rejection of that idea. רב מנשה's words, which carry the rejection, come on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know the רבנן were lenient in testimony about a husband's death, for example by accepting a single witness. So one might think they would accept even a רשע there. By saying 'but didn't רב מנשה say,' the גמרא signals that this leniency does not go that far. The proof itself comes in רב מנשה's statement.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say. Introduces a possible answer that the גמרא is about to reject.
Testimony that a woman's husband died, so she may remarry.
The רבנן were lenient. They relaxed the usual rules of testimony.

phrases.english: And if you would say:
testimony for a woman is different,
since the Rabbis were lenient with it —
but didn't Rav Menashe say:
phrases.notes: רב מנשה's actual words are on the next amud. They will show that even here a רשע is not accepted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: שָׁאנֵי עֵדוּת אִשָּׁה דַּאֲקִילּוּ בַּהּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a possible answer to the challenge of step 28 and begins knocking it out.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggested answer that the leniency of עדות אשה would let even a self-declared רשע testify.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב מנשה's statement, which continues on the next amud, will show that the leniency of עדות אשה does not include accepting a רשע.
